intro:
By the end of this track you can look at a data job and say what it will cost before it runs: how many bytes it reads after skipping partitions and columns, how many stages and tasks Spark will run and where the shuffles fall, which join it will pick, and whether it needs a cluster at all. You can lay out payments data as Parquet in an Apache Iceberg table, correct it with `MERGE INTO`, keep it fast with compaction and snapshot expiry, stream into it from Kafka exactly once with event-time windows and watermarks, and choose between DuckDB, Spark, Trino and a streaming engine with numbers instead of habit.

You need to read Kotlin or Java and have JDK 21 installed; the Gradle wrapper fetches everything else. You don't need a cluster, Hadoop or Docker. Spark 4.1 (the newest line both Iceberg 1.12 and Delta Lake 4.4 support), Iceberg and DuckDB run inside the test JVM on your laptop. No earlier track is required, though the operating systems track's page cache and the Kafka track's offsets come up as reminders.

The labs live in `labs/bigdata`, one package per lesson (`sfz.bigdata.l01` to `l12`), in Kotlin. Each lab is a small model or a real Spark, Iceberg or DuckDB program that the tests check against generated, deterministic payments data: run `./gradlew :bigdata:test --tests 'sfz.bigdata.l05.*'` from the `labs` folder, and `./gradlew :bigdata:demo -Pmain=...` for the Try-it demos. The tests share one local Spark session (two worker threads, four shuffle partitions), so the first test of a run pays a few seconds of start-up. Timings in the lessons were measured on a busy laptop: trust the ratios and the shapes, not the milliseconds.
cheatsheet:
## Cost of a scan (lessons 1 and 12)

`time = bytes read / bandwidth of the slowest stage` (disk, network or CPU decoding). 1 TB at 500 MB/s is 2,000 s. Two levers: more readers (split into blocks, run in parallel) and fewer bytes (columns, compression, skipping). Pull "fewer bytes" first.

| Step | Example: 4 TB, 3 years, 60 columns |
|---|---|
| Partitions read | 30 of 1,095 days: 110 GB |
| Columns read | 4 of 60: 7.3 GB |
| One machine's speed | min(cores x decode rate, storage rate): 3 GB/s laptop, about 1.5 GB/s VM from S3 |
| Users sharing it | time x concurrent queries |
| Working set | join build side or groups; must fit in RAM |

Route: fits one machine in time and memory: DuckDB. Otherwise a cluster sized by max(time / budget, working set / RAM): Trino if seconds-scale and interactive, Spark if a long batch job. Never-ending work: Structured Streaming or Flink.

## What survived from Hadoop and Hive (lessons 2 and 3)

- HDFS: files in 128 MiB blocks, 3 replicas, a NameNode holding the block map. MapReduce: map, partition by `hash(key) mod R`, shuffle to local disk, fetch and sort, reduce. A combiner pre-aggregates only for associative and commutative work; for an average carry `(sum, count)`.
- Hive: a table is a directory plus a schema in the metastore; partitions are `dt=2026-11-07/` folders. Pruning works only on the partition column. Folders written behind the metastore's back need `MSCK REPAIR TABLE`. Writes aren't atomic and small files cost an open each.

## Parquet (lesson 4)

Row groups, each with one column chunk per column, made of pages; a footer at the end with offsets and min/max/null counts, then its 4-byte length and `PAR1`. Dictionary, RLE and delta encodings, then Snappy or Zstd. Min/max skip row groups only when data is sorted or clustered on the filter column. `PushedFilters` lists what Spark offered, not what was skipped; Spark writes `INT96` timestamps by default, and those skip nothing.

## Spark execution (lessons 5 to 7)

| Concept | Rule |
|---|---|
| Lazy plan | transformations build a plan; actions (`count`, `collect`, `write`) run it, each time |
| Narrow vs wide | `where`, `select`, `withColumn` chain in one task; `groupBy`, `join`, `distinct`, `repartition` need an `Exchange` |
| Stages | one input: stages = Exchanges + 1; tasks = partitions; extra tasks wait in waves |
| Failure | a task is retried up to 4 times from lineage; lost shuffle files rerun their map tasks |
| Shuffle | each map task writes one file with a block per reducer: M x R blocks |
| `repartition(n)` vs `coalesce(n)` | shuffle to n even partitions vs merge without a shuffle (and the stage before runs as n tasks) |
| `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` | 200 by default; with AQE on, set it high and let AQE merge |
| Joins | sort-merge: shuffle both sides by key. Broadcast hash: copy the small side everywhere, under 10 MB by estimate, or force with `broadcast()` |
| AQE | re-plans at each shuffle with real sizes: merges small partitions, switches to broadcast, splits skewed partitions (over 5x median and 256 MB) |
| Skew | one hot key, one slow task: broadcast, let AQE split, or salt the key |
| `cache()` | pays only when reused; cache after the filter, `unpersist()` after |

Read plans with `explain("formatted")`: `Exchange hashpartitioning`, `BroadcastExchange`, `SortMergeJoin`, `AQEShuffleRead`, `InMemoryTableScan`.

## Spark 4 for JVM engineers (lesson 8)

Spark Connect: the client sends unresolved plans over gRPC (port 15002) and gets Arrow batches; no SparkContext, no RDDs. ANSI mode is on: bad casts, overflow and division by zero fail; use `try_cast`, `try_add`, `try_divide` where null is intended. VARIANT holds parsed JSON (`parse_json`, `variant_get`). From Kotlin, prefer column expressions or SQL; typed lambdas hide logic from Catalyst.

## File format, table format, catalog (lessons 9 and 10)

| Layer | Example | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| File format | Parquet | rows of one file, by column, with stats |
| Table format | Iceberg, Delta, Hudi | which files make each version of a table, schemas, partition specs, snapshots |
| Catalog | Hadoop folder, JDBC, Hive Metastore, REST (Polaris, Unity Catalog) | the pointer to each table's current metadata; the commit's compare-and-swap |

Iceberg: pointer, then `vN.metadata.json`, then a manifest list per snapshot, then manifests with per-file stats, then Parquet. A commit writes new files and swaps the pointer if it still names the base; the loser retries. `VERSION AS OF` / `TIMESTAMP AS OF` until snapshots expire. Columns have ids (rename is metadata only); `PARTITIONED BY (days(created_at))` is hidden partitioning.

| Row-level change | Writes | Reads |
|---|---|---|
| copy-on-write (default) | rewrites every file with a changed row | plain files |
| merge-on-read, v2 | new rows + position delete files (file, row) | merge deletes |
| merge-on-read, v3 | new rows + one deletion vector per data file (Puffin) | one bitmap per file |

Maintenance, in order: `rewrite_data_files` (compaction, a `replace` snapshot), `expire_snapshots` (5 days and 1 snapshot kept by default; ends time travel), `remove_orphan_files` (3 days by default, refuses under 24 hours).

## Streaming (lesson 11)

Count by event time, not processing time. `withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")` on the window's column, before `groupBy(window(...))`. Watermark = latest event time seen minus the delay, applied from the next micro-batch. A window is final when the watermark reaches its end; an event is dropped only if its window has closed.

| Output mode | Writes | State |
|---|---|---|
| append | each row once, when final | cleaned by watermark |
| update | rows changed in this batch | cleaned by watermark |
| complete | the whole result, every batch | never cleaned |

Exactly once = replayable source (Kafka offsets) + checkpoint (`offsets/`, `commits/`, `state/`) + idempotent or transactional sink (Iceberg records the batch id; `foreachBatch` must use it). Real-time Mode: Spark 4.1 stateless, 4.3 stateful, Kafka only. Flink: streaming-first, large keyed state.

## Engines (lesson 12)

| Engine | Use it for |
|---|---|
| DuckDB | anything one machine reads in time: ad hoc, reports, tests; reads Parquet and Iceberg in place |
| Spark | long batch jobs, backfills, big joins and shuffles, Structured Streaming |
| Trino | interactive SQL for many users over the lake and other sources |
| ClickHouse | sub-second queries on fresh events, in its own storage |
| Flink | streaming as the product: per-event latency, very large state |
| Airflow 3 | orchestration; DAGs triggered when assets (tables) change |
recap: A scan costs the bytes it reads over the slowest stage's bandwidth. Read fewer bytes (columns, compression, partitions, min/max) before you add machines, and size every job by its bytes after pruning, not by the size of the table.

The ideas that survived Hadoop are blocks read in parallel, map then shuffle by key then reduce, and partitions as folders. Hive's metastore became the first catalog, and its non-atomic folders are why table formats exist.

Parquet stores each column apart with min/max per row group in a footer, so engines read only the columns and row groups a query can use, and only if the data is sorted or clustered on the filter column.
Spark builds a lazy plan, Catalyst optimizes it, and executors run one task per partition. Every wide step adds a shuffle and a stage. AQE re-plans at each shuffle with real sizes.
Most Spark tuning is about the shuffle: how many partitions, whether a join broadcasts its small side or sort-merges both, and whether one hot key turns one task into the whole job.
Spark 4 runs clients over Connect, fails bad data loudly in ANSI mode, and stores JSON as VARIANT.

An Iceberg table is Parquet files plus a tree of metadata, committed by a compare-and-swap in a catalog. That gives atomic commits, snapshots and time travel, safe schema and partition changes, and row-level corrections by copy-on-write or merge-on-read, kept healthy by compaction and snapshot expiry.

Streams are grouped by event time. A watermark decides when a window is final and bounds state, the output mode decides what each batch writes, and exactly once needs a replayable source, a checkpoint and an idempotent sink.

With one copy of the data in an open table format behind a catalog, each workload picks its engine by the numbers: DuckDB when one machine is enough, Trino for shared interactive SQL, Spark for heavy batch, a streaming engine for continuous work.

quiz.q: A 5 TB payments table holds 2 years of daily partitions and 50 columns of similar size. An analyst's query reads 5 columns of the last 10 days. Which estimate should drive the choice of engine?
options: 5 TB, the size of the table
About 68 GB, the last 10 days
About 6.8 GB: 10 of 730 days and 5 of 50 columns, a few seconds on one machine
The number of rows, because engines process rows
quiz.why: 5 TB x 10 / 730 = 68 GB for the days, x 5 / 50 = 6.8 GB for the columns. At 2 to 3 GB/s that's a few seconds on one machine, so DuckDB is enough. Sizing by the table's 5 TB is the mistake lessons 1 and 12 both warn about; 68 GB forgets that Parquet reads only the columns a query uses.

quiz.q: A MapReduce job computes the average amount per merchant. To shrink the shuffle you add a combiner. What must the map and combine steps emit?
options: A (sum, count) pair per merchant, which the reducer adds up and divides at the end
The average of each map task's amounts, which the reducer averages again
Every amount unchanged, because averages can't be combined
The maximum amount, which bounds the average
quiz.why: A combiner is safe only for associative and commutative work. An average of averages is wrong when map tasks see different numbers of rows; sums and counts add correctly, and the reducer divides once. Sending every amount is correct but throws away the combiner's saving.

quiz.q: A Hive table is partitioned by a `dt` string column; an Iceberg table is `PARTITIONED BY (days(created_at))`. Both get `WHERE created_at >= '2026-11-01' AND created_at < '2026-11-02'`. What happens?
options: Both prune to one day
Neither prunes, because the filter is on a timestamp
The Hive table prunes, Iceberg doesn't, because Iceberg has no partition folders
The Hive table reads every partition, because the filter isn't on `dt`; Iceberg derives the day from `created_at` and reads one
quiz.why: In Hive the partition value lives only in the `dt` folder name, so only a filter on `dt` can skip folders. Iceberg's hidden partitioning records that each file's partition is `day(created_at)`, so a range on `created_at` becomes a range of days and the other days' files are skipped from the manifests.

quiz.q: Which sentence puts Parquet, Iceberg and an Iceberg REST catalog such as Apache Polaris in the right roles?
options: Parquet is the table format, Iceberg the file format, Polaris the query engine
Parquet stores rows by column inside one file; Iceberg lists which files make up each version of a table; Polaris holds each table's current-metadata pointer and swaps it on commit
Iceberg is a database that stores Parquet; Polaris is its backup
All three are query engines that read the same files
quiz.why: A file format describes bytes inside one file (columns, row groups, footer statistics). A table format describes a table as a set of such files, with snapshots, schemas and partition specs. The catalog maps names to each table's current metadata and makes commits atomic with a compare-and-swap. None of them runs queries; Spark, Trino and DuckDB do.

quiz.q: A job reads Parquet, filters by status, adds a column with `withColumn`, groups by merchant and counts. With one input and AQE off, how many stages does the count action run?
options: 1, because Spark fuses everything
3: one per transformation type
2: the narrow steps run in one stage, and the `groupBy` adds a shuffle that starts a second
4: one per step
quiz.why: Filter and `withColumn` are narrow: each output partition depends on one input partition, so they chain inside the same task as the scan. `groupBy` is wide: rows with the same merchant must meet, so Spark inserts an `Exchange`, which ends a stage. For one input, stages = Exchanges + 1 = 2.

quiz.q: A filter over 2,000 input partitions leaves little data, and you want 20 output files. With `coalesce(20)` the whole job got slow. Why, and what fixes it?
options: `coalesce` has no shuffle, so it pulls the stage before it, the filter, down to 20 tasks; `repartition(20)` adds a shuffle but lets the filter keep 2,000 tasks
`coalesce` shuffles everything; use `repartition(20)`, which doesn't
20 files is too few; write 2,000 files
`coalesce` only works on cached data
quiz.why: `coalesce(n)` merges partitions without a shuffle, so there's no stage boundary: the scan and filter run in the same 20 tasks, each reading 100 input partitions. `repartition(20)` costs a shuffle of the filtered (small) data, but the expensive scan keeps its 2,000-way parallelism. That's the trade lesson 6 measured.

quiz.q: A join of 2 billion payments with a merchants table is planned as `SortMergeJoin` because the optimizer estimated the filtered merchants side at 40 MB. At run time it turns out to be 2 MB. What does Spark 4 do by default?
options: Keeps the sort-merge join; plans never change once they start
Fails, because the estimate was wrong
Broadcasts the 2 billion payments instead
AQE sees the real 2 MB after the shuffle stage and switches the join to a broadcast hash join, skipping the shuffle of the big side
quiz.why: The static plan is chosen from estimates, and after a filter the estimate is often the whole input, so it lands above the 10 MB broadcast threshold. AQE, on by default, re-plans at each shuffle with real sizes and converts the join to a broadcast hash join when one side turns out small. You can also force it with `broadcast()` when you know better than the estimate.

quiz.q: After upgrading to Spark 4, a nightly job fails on `CAST(amount AS DECIMAL(12,2))` because some rows hold `"12,50"`. What's the right fix?
options: Set `spark.sql.ansi.enabled=false` so bad casts return NULL again
Use `try_cast` for that column and route rows where it returns NULL to a quarantine table
Cast to STRING instead
Retry the job until it passes
quiz.why: Spark 4 turned ANSI mode on, so an invalid cast fails the query instead of silently returning NULL. Switching ANSI off brings back silent data loss for every column. `try_cast` returns NULL on purpose for just this expression, and quarantining those rows keeps them visible. Retrying can't fix bad input.

quiz.q: A correction feed updates a few hundred payments every 5 minutes in an Iceberg table of 512 MB files. Reads happen all day. Which setup fits, and what must come with it?
options: Merge-on-read (deletion vectors on format v3), plus scheduled compaction and snapshot expiry
Copy-on-write, with no maintenance needed
Appending corrected rows and deduplicating in every query
A new table for every batch
quiz.why: Copy-on-write would rewrite every 512 MB file that holds a changed row, every 5 minutes. Merge-on-read writes small files of new rows plus deletes, and readers merge them. Without compaction those pile up and reads slow down, and without expiry the old files never leave the bucket.

quiz.q: A fraud rule counts authorizations per merchant per 5 minutes. The consumer was down from 10:10 to 10:20, then read the backlog in a minute. Which statement is right?
options: Counting by processing time is safer, because it never waits for late data
Both give the same counts once the backlog is read
Counting by event time puts each authorization in the window it happened in, and a watermark decides when each window is final; counting by arrival makes the backlog a fake spike at 10:20
A watermark makes processing-time counts correct
quiz.why: Processing time is when the consumer read the event, so an outage empties some windows and floods the next. Event time is when the card was used, carried in the event, so the counts match reality whenever the events arrive. The watermark is what makes event-time windows finish: latest event time minus the allowed delay. It doesn't fix processing-time counts.
